description: With 21 number of publications, the first cluster (in red) is labelled ‘Innovation Ecosystems and Knowledge Transfer in Institutional Contexts.’ This cluster highlights how innovation ecosystem’s function and evolve through institutional mechanisms such as knowledge transfer, intellectual property strategies, and intermediary support. Key studies explore the conceptual foundation of innovation ecosystems (Gomes et  al., 2018), the role of returnee entrepreneurs in high-tech SME performance (Filatotchev et  al., 2009), and intellectual property dynamics (Holgersson et  al., 2018). Moreover, other works emphasize absorptive capacity in university-led quadruple helix ecosystems (Miller et  al., 2016), value co-creation between academia and business (Clarysse et  al., 2014), and how entrepreneurs leverage institutional intermediaries in emerging economies (Armanios et  al., 2017). Together, these studies underscore the strategic importance of institutional alignment, collaboration, and support in enhancing innovation outcomes.

The second cluster (in green) comprises 13 publications labelled as ‘Business Incubators and Entrepreneurial Ecosystems.’ This cluster examines how incubators, science parks, and ecosystem structures support entrepreneurial development. Rubin et  al. (2015) emphasizes the role of knowledge flow and stakeholder interactions in technological incubators. McAdam and McAdam (2008) highlight how incubator resource use aligns with start-up lifecycle stages. Also, Nicotra et  al. (2018) offer a framework linking ecosystem elements, such as governance and networks, to productive entrepreneurship. To sum up, these studies highlight the importance of structured support systems and collaborative dynamics in fostering entrepreneurial success.

The third cluster (in blue) is labelled as ‘Strategic Roles of Universities in Innovation and Impact’ with 10 publications. This cluster focuses on how universities contribute to innovation ecosystems through entrepreneurship, knowledge exchange, and technology transfer. Rothaermel et  al. (2007) develop a taxonomy of university entrepreneurship literature, identifying key streams including entrepreneurial universities, technology transfer offices, and spin-off creation. Phan and Siegel (2006) assess the effectiveness of university technology transfer mechanisms, highlighting the need for improved incentives, infrastructure, and faculty engagement. Furthermore, Hughes and Kitson (2012) provide empirical evidence on the strategic role of universities in the UK, showing how institutional constraints and regional factors influence the breadth and depth of knowledge exchange activities. Collectively, these studies emphasize the evolving mission of universities as drivers of economic and societal impact through structured innovation strategies.

The fourth cluster (in yellow) is labelled as ‘Entrepreneurial Universities and Academic Ecosystems’ with three publications. Hayter et  al. (2018) provide an extensive review and conceptual development of academic entrepreneurship ecosystems, outlining key components such as actors, relationships, and environmental conditions that shape university-based entrepreneurship. Abreu et  al. (2016) compare entrepreneurial practices between research-intensive and teaching-led universities, revealing distinct patterns in how different types of institutions engage in entrepreneurial activities and interact with external stakeholders. Guerrero et  al. (2016) explore emerging models of entrepreneurial universities within shifting social and economic contexts, emphasizing institutional adaptability, mission evolution, and strategic partnerships. To sum up, these studies contribute to a deeper understanding of how universities are evolving into dynamic entrepreneurial ecosystems that respond to changing societal demands.
